patch.value: Do not print the personal address or username in public issue text. This blocker is independent of pm-todos-x5my implementation correctness and pm-todos-qpst coverage.
Reachable history contains personal identities and absolute host-path evidence

A full reachable-history audit found package-owned PM patches containing absolute home paths and commit metadata containing non-noreply personal identity domains. Current tracked source has no absolute home paths, private IPs, or private keys, and current credential-pattern hits are benign variable/control names, but current cleanliness does not remove reachable historical disclosure.

Produce a value-redacted path/commit inventory; obtain explicit maintainer authorization for retain versus coordinated rewrite; if rewriting, preserve PM semantic history and retag/review every affected release; rerun current tracked, full patch, full blob, author-identity, npm tarball, and GitHub secret scans; record exact post-remediation counts and external coordination; prohibit merge/publication while unresolved

Count absolute-home pattern patch lines under .agents/pm across git log --all -p without printing values; count commit author emails outside users.noreply.github.com by domain; inspect affected paths with usernames redacted.

Every public reachable commit and PM history stream is cleared for personal/private data, or the maintainer explicitly accepts named residual metadata after reviewing a value-redacted inventory. Any authorized rewrite preserves release/tag provenance and is followed by fresh current/history scans, package gates, remote review, and coordinated publication decisions.

Two package-owned PM records retain absolute home-path evidence across reachable patches: one test-command record and one prior readiness note/history stream. The reachable commit graph has 97 commits using a personal-domain author email and one localhost identity. Historical vendored dependencies also contain generic private-IP and email fixtures. No private-key pattern was found. No history rewrite is authorized, so merge and publication remain blocked.

Publishing or republishing from the current graph continues distributing avoidable personal identity and host-layout metadata; rewriting without authorization could instead break tags, forks, and consumers.
